questions.q: What fundamentally distinguishes a simple chat turn from an agent?
options: An agent always uses a bigger model with more parameters
A simple chat turn is one request and one reply with no loop; an agent can take an action, observe the result, and decide its next action across multiple steps
Simple chat can never produce long answers
An agent never produces any text output at all
questions.explain: Plain chat stops after one reply. An agent is given tools and permission to keep running, deciding turn by turn what to do next based on what just happened.

questions.q: In Anthropic's own distinction between a 'workflow' and an 'agent', what is the key difference?
options: A workflow follows a path your code controls step by step; an agent is a system where the model itself decides, turn by turn, which action to take next
There is no meaningful difference between the two terms
A workflow always uses more tools than an agent
An agent can never be combined with a workflow
questions.explain: The line is about who is driving: predefined code paths (workflow) versus the model directing its own process and tool use (agent).

questions.q: Why can't a pure chat model reliably answer a question like 'what's our current refund policy,' per this lesson's example?
options: Chat models are incapable of answering any factual question
The policy text may not already be in its context, so it can only guess or admit it doesn't know — it has no way to go check
Refund policy questions are always outside any model's training data
Only agents are allowed to discuss company policies
questions.explain: Without a tool call and a loop to use it, a chat-only model is stuck with whatever's already in its context — it can't go look something up and incorporate the result.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe agency as 'a spectrum, not a binary label'?
options: Because only systems with ten or more tools count as agents
Because agency has nothing to do with tool count or looping
Because every chatbot is automatically a full multi-agent system
Because a system calling exactly one tool and stopping is more agentic than plain chat but far simpler than one that loops many times, reflects, or coordinates other agents
questions.explain: There's a real range between one-shot chat and a fully looping, reflecting, multi-agent system — most real systems sit somewhere in between.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about whether more agency is always better?
options: More agency is always strictly better with no downsides
Agency should be maximized in every system regardless of the task
More agency trades off against latency, cost, and new ways to fail — which is why a later lesson covers when agents are overkill
Agency has no cost implications at all
questions.explain: Looping, tool-calling systems take longer, cost more per task, and introduce new failure modes (like looping wrong) — a tradeoff worth making only when the task actually needs it.
